title: Spin-Wave Phase Shifter Controlled by a Domain Wall Racetrack
authors: Uladzislau Makartsou, Olena Tartakivska, Paweł Gruszecki, Anton Lutsenko, Sebastiaan van Dijken, Volodymyr V. Kruglyak, Maciej Krawczyk
abstract: We propose a spin-wave phase shifter controlled using a domain-wall racetrack. The concept is demonstrated using micromagnetic simulations of a Permalloy domain-wall racetrack placed above a YIG film. The stray field from pinned domain walls modifies the internal magnetic field in the YIG region under the racetrack. This leads to a local change of the spin-wave wavelength and thereby enables control of the phase accumulated by Damon-Eshbach spin waves propagating through the region. Moving domain walls on the racetrack, the same physical structure can provide phase shifts of up to +/-90 degrees, without changing the waveguide geometry. A model based on the semiclassical approximation confirms that the phase shift is dominated by the domain-wall-induced stray field. These results suggest a route toward a compact programmable spin-wave phase shifter for interference-based magnonic circuits for information processing. Moreover, the demonstrated magnonic device integration with a magnetic domain-wall racetrack can lead to its application in in-memory computing.
summary: This work proposes a novel spin-wave phase shifter by integrating a domain-wall racetrack into a magnonic waveguide. By exploiting the stray field from magnetic domain walls, researchers can induce large, controllable phase shifts ($\pm 90^\circ$) for propagating spin waves. This demonstrates a scalable route toward functional elements for information processing in magnonics.
main_problem: The goal is to develop a compact, programmable spin-wave phase shifter for magnonic circuits by utilizing the stray field generated by magnetic domain walls.
main_result: Moving domain walls on a racetrack structure can induce significant and tunable phase shifts (up to $\pm 90^\circ$) in propagating Damon-Eshbach spin waves without altering the waveguide's physical geometry.
method: The analysis relies heavily on micromagnetic simulations (MuMax3) complemented by semi-analytical models using the Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin (WKB) approximation to calculate phase accumulation.
model_or_system: The system consists of a YIG film waveguide patterned with a Permalloy ($	ext{Py}$) domain-wall racetrack. The stray field from pinned magnetic domain walls modifies the internal effective magnetic field experienced by the spin waves propagating in the YIG layer.
key_observables: Spin-wave phase shift ($\Delta\varphi$), SW wavelength change, and SW intensity attenuation ($\Delta A_{SW}$).
important_parameters: Bias fields (e.g., $-15 	ext{ mT}$), operating frequencies (2.5–5 GHz), and material parameters for YIG and Py.
main_assumptions: The WKB model assumes slowly-varying fields, and the analysis often focuses on a single central 1D slice approximation of the stray field profile.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry (Py racetrack over YIG), dispersion relations comparing bare vs. DW-modified waveguides, and spatial profiles of effective magnetic fields ($B_{	ext{eff},z}$) showing the influence of domain walls.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical setup (racetrack/DW interaction), developing theoretical models (WKB approximation for phase shift calculation), presenting simulation results comparing DW-induced shifts to simpler stripe geometries, and concluding with the potential application in magnonic circuits.
why_interesting: While focused on classical magnetism, the concept of using engineered magnetic structures to control wave propagation phases is analogous to controlling quantum beam paths or implementing non-linear phase gates in photonic/quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Geometry and magnetic configuration of the simu- lated phase shifter. (a) Three-dimensional view of the model: A Py racetrack of 50 nm width and 20 nm thickness is sep- arated by 5 nm from a 50 nm thick YIG film. A static bias magnetic field of Bext = −15 mT is applied along the z-axis. SWs propagate in the YIG film along the x-direction. The SW phase evaluated before and after the Py stripe is shown by φin and φout, respectively. Black arrows indicate the equi- librium magnetization in YIG. (b) Micromagnetic state of the Py stripe: The magnetization in the central domain between the two notches located 320 nm apart is antiparallel to that in the outer parts of the stripe.

FIG. 2. Selecting the operating frequency regime. (a,b) Dispersion of a bare YIG film (blue) and YIG/Py bilayer (red) for two orientations of the magnetization in the Py layer: (a) parallel and (b) antiparallel to the magnetization of YIG. (c) The SW phase shift ∆φ induced by a uniformly magnetized Py stripe is shown as a function of the stripe’s width w for the parallel and antiparallel orientations of the stripe’s magnetization relative to that of YIG, the bias magnetic field Bext = −15 mT and the frequency f = 2.8 GHz. The transparent blue regions indicate the working frequency and width ranges.

FIG. 3. Magnetization and effective-field landscapes underlying the DW-induced phase shifts. (a,e) Equilibrium magnetization texture in the YIG layer for (a) 010 and (e) 101 racetrack configurations shown in panels (b) and (f), respectively, for the racetrack width w = 50 nm and magnetic field Bext = −15 mT along the z-axis. The displayed magnetization maps correspond to the top surfaces of the YIG film and the racetrack. (c,g) Corresponding maps of the effective field component Beff,z in the YIG film with the stray field of the racetrack.
